headline: The S&P 500 rose 2.5% this week, but it ended badly: the 10 year closed at 5.15%, QQQ fell back under its 683.69 line and its 200 day, and Nvidia lost 12.75% after its CEO quit. Next week Nvidia reports Tuesday, Anthropic prices Wednesday and Trump meets Xi and Putin Thursday in China.
summary: Prices are Friday Nov 13 closes. The dashboard (prices_as_of 2026-11-13) and Massive agree on the setups and most buy list names, but 26 of 83 long term names still carry Nov 12 closes; those are corrected here from Massive. For the week SPY rose 2.59% to 754.37 and QQQ 3.63% to 679.89, but QQQ fell 1.20% Friday and closed 0.56% under its 683.69 line (Massive). Rates did the damage: the 10 year rose about 29 basis points in a week to 5.15%, its highest close since Oct 19, after hot core CPI, two weak long bond sales and a 6.5% yearly rise in producer prices (Forbes; FactIQ; New York Post). Nvidia fell 12.75% for the week to 162.85 after its CEO resigned, while AMD gained 18.93% even after an 8.75% drop Friday (Massive). The scorecard still shows 4 finished swings (3 wins, +0.12R average), no finished puts, and one clear lesson: long term buys in the AI groups trail the S&P 500 by 18.7 points at 20 days. No PMCC passes this week, no phone alert fired, and the only live swing setup is TMO.

regime.why: The indexes rose for the week and the VIX fell 24.7% to 19.30, but QQQ closed under its correction line and its 200 day on Friday, and the 10 year at 5.15% is the highest since October. A December hike is close to fully priced, so there is no rate cushion. Breadth was better than the index: the equal weight S&P 500 fund rose 2.37% for the week.

signals.title: Week in review: a green week with a weak finish; rates and Nvidia set the tone
signals.since_yesterday: Friday: QQQ fell 1.20% and closed back under 683.69, AMD gave back 8.75% and Cisco 6.24%, while the 10 year closed at 5.15%.
signals.what_happened: Week of Nov 9 to 13, Massive closes Nov 6 to Nov 13: SPY +2.59% (754.37), QQQ +3.63% (679.89), DIA +2.13%, IWM +1.41%, SMH +4.91%, XLE +5.42%, XLF +2.66%, XLV +2.19%, XLU +2.11%, XLP +2.52%, RSP (equal weight) +2.37%, GLD -4.58%, TLT -3.10%, IBIT -9.19%. Biggest moves on the dashboard's maps: AMD +18.93%, AVGO +18.16%, ANET +15.51%, ENTG +15.18%, CRWV +14.50%, MU +12.80%, MP +9.46%, CAT +7.44%; NVDA -12.75% (162.85), BABA -13.77%, HIMS -24.12%. The days: Monday a thin rebound; Tuesday core CPI 0.3% against 0.2% expected and a tailed 10 year sale at 5.02%; Wednesday CoreWeave beat and QQQ closed over 683.69 on light volume; Thursday Nvidia's CEO resigned and the 30 year sale tailed at 5.441%; Friday producer prices rose 0.3% against 0.4% expected, but 6.5% from a year ago, and the 10 year still closed at 5.15% (New York Post; Forbes). On Friday QQQ fell 1.20% on 42.1 million shares, under its 45.3 million 30 day average (Massive; TradingView), AMD fell 8.75% to 534.06 and Cisco 6.24% to 95.64 as a 250 basis point gross margin squeeze outweighed record revenue (Benzinga). The S&P 500 index rose about 2.5% for the week (IBD).
signals.so_what: Money moved out of Nvidia and into its rivals early in the week, then came back out of those rivals on Friday. That is rotation, not a new uptrend. The bigger force is the price of money: a 10 year at 5.15% competes directly with stocks, raises mortgage and corporate borrowing costs, and hits the long duration tech names first. Second order: weak Treasury sales mean buyers want more yield to hold US debt, so every auction now matters to stocks. Third order: banks and energy held up (XLF +2.66%, XLE +5.42%), the groups that do better when rates and oil stay high. What would make this wrong: a calm retail sales number Tuesday and a clean Nvidia guide could pull yields and tech back together.
signals.for_you: Swing: no new longs. QQQ closed 679.89, under its 683.69 line and its 200 day, on below average volume. Puts: the weekday screen resumes Monday; the bar is now about 5.15% a year. Long term: in zone names only in small first tranches, and not before Nvidia reports Nov 17.

signals.title: Scorecard: how the calls did
signals.what_happened: Graded Nov 14 on Nov 13 data (site/data/scorecard.json). Swings, graded by her rule (a trigger is a close over the entry on at least 1.5 times the 50 day volume; the fill is that close; a win is a close at the target): 22 calls, 4 finished, 3 wins (ABBV +0.25R, LNG +0.36R, BDX +0.86R), 1 loss (EOG -1.0R), average +0.12R, the same as last week. 16 never triggered, 1 open (WST, filled at 416.41, closed 416.42, so 0.00R), 1 waiting (TMO from Nov 4). PFE and AMGN were open and under water last week; they now count as never triggered because each closed under its stop before its confirming close, the rule fix made after COP. Cash secured puts: 24 logged, none finished; the first 10 expire Nov 20. Long term buys: 124 calls; 54 of 120 beat SPY after 5 days (45%, average 2.55 points behind) and 43 of 102 after 20 days (42%, average 3.81 points behind), worse than last week's 49% and 0.54 behind. Brief signals: 229 calls; 98 of 182 right after 5 days (54%, average 0.10 behind) and 51 of 90 after 20 days (57%, average 2.41 ahead). Split of the 102 long term calls with 20 day results (my math from the scorecard and the theme maps): 34 in the AI compute or AI power maps averaged 18.68 points behind SPY and only 3 beat it; the other 68 averaged 3.62 points ahead and 40 beat it.
signals.so_what: Swings: 4 finished calls prove nothing, so read the swing record as 'no edge shown yet'. What works: the volume rule and the new void rule kept the dashboard out of 16 setups, many of which then fell. Brief signals are now 57% right at 20 days and 2.41 points ahead of SPY. What does not work: long term buys made in the AI groups in early October, right before those groups fell 25% to 40%. Those 34 calls are not 34 independent tests; they are mostly one bad week, so the sample is smaller than it looks. Even so, the gap (18.7 points behind against 3.6 ahead) is too large to ignore, and it has lasted about six weeks. If it lasts two months (early December), the routine says to change the rule.
signals.for_you: One rule change to consider: add a group check to the long term 'Buy zone now' verdict. Only rate a name 'Buy zone now' when its group is not falling, for example its group ETF (SMH for chips, XLU for utilities) is above its 50 day average or not down more than 8% in a month. The put rules already say to avoid falling groups; this makes the long term buys match. Last week's chase limit idea (skip a swing trigger more than 5% over the entry) stays in tracking only. Puts: Nov 20 is expiration week; the three logged brief ideas expiring that day (PFE $27, C $120, JPM $310) all closed above their strikes on Nov 13 (cushions 7.0%, 3.3% and 11.7%).

signals.what_happened: First weekly check under the Nov 7 decision (Saturdays only, only names with an active long dated option market; decide Dec 5 whether to drop). Of the 12 names on the Nov 13 'Buy zone now' list, only AMD and PFE have long dated calls that traded on Nov 13 (Massive daily bars). AMD: in its zone (534.06, zone 525.17 to 571.19), no dividend, next report Feb 2, 2027 (TradingView, unconfirmed), so a Dec 18 or Dec 31 short call would be clear of earnings. But its Jan 2028 $400 call traded only 45 contracts with a day range of about 18% of its price, and the stock fell 8.75% in one day. PFE: in its zone (28.89, zone 25.41 to 29.29), last ex dividend Nov 6, next not yet declared (it was Jan 23 last year), next report Feb 2, 2027 (unconfirmed). Its Jan 2028 $22 call traded 25 contracts in 8 trades. The rest fail earlier: ADI reports Nov 24 and SNPS Dec 8 (inside a short call's life); GD, LDOS, AEP, SEI, ENTG, PODD and RELY had no long dated call market worth testing, and RELY is in a falling group; PYPL's true Nov 13 close (59.28) is above its zone. No premium is quoted here.
signals.so_what: Week 1 of the weekly check gives the same answer as the 10 day trial: no example. The two names with real option markets show the problem. AMD's options trade, but its moves are huge, and a PMCC's long call loses about twice the stock's percentage drop. PFE is calm, but its long dated calls barely trade, so the price you pay for the long leg is a guess.
signals.for_you: No PMCC this week. Closest call: PFE (target long call about 0.80 delta, 9 to 15 months out; short call about 0.30 delta, 30 to 45 days out, strike above the long strike plus the debit; check the chain and skip it if the spread is wide). Worst case: the long call can lose about twice the stock's percentage drop. Log for review: days a candidate passed since Oct 24: none. Next check Saturday Nov 21; the drop decision is Dec 5.

signals.title: Rates: the 10 year closed at 5.15%; a December hike is close to fully priced
signals.since_yesterday: Friday's close: the 10 year rose 5 basis points to 5.15% even though producer prices came in a tenth under forecast; the 2 year closed at 4.88%.
signals.what_happened: The 10 year Treasury yield closed at 5.15% on Nov 13, up 5 basis points on the day and about 29 basis points on the week, its highest since Oct 19; it touched 5.17% during the day (Forbes; FactIQ; Yahoo Finance). The 2 year closed at 4.88% and the 30 year at 5.47% (Forbes). October producer prices rose 0.3% against 0.4% expected but 6.5% from a year earlier (New York Post). After the data, CME FedWatch showed about an 88% to 90% chance of a quarter point hike on Dec 9 (AP via iHeart; InvestmentNews via Admiral Markets); CNBC's live blog said 100%. The Fed's range is 3.75% to 4.00% (New York Post).
signals.so_what: The 2 year jumped about 42 basis points in a week, so the market has moved from 'maybe a hike' to 'a hike is coming'. When short rates jump faster than long ones, it is the Fed being priced, not growth. Who pays: borrowers, small caps with floating debt, homebuilders, and long duration tech. Who gets paid: savers and banks with cheap deposits. What would make this wrong: a soft retail sales number Tuesday or dovish words in Wednesday's Fed minutes.
signals.for_you: Puts: a 5.15% 10 year raises the bar; a put must now pay more than about 5.15% a year to be worth the risk. Swing: avoid rate sensitive names into Tuesday's retail sales and Wednesday's 20 year sale. Long term: no change to the buy list from rates alone.

signals.title: Nvidia into Tuesday's report: about ten downgrades to Hold, the stock is oversold, estimates have not fallen
signals.since_yesterday: HSBC cut NVDA to Hold with a $170 target (from $365) on Friday, and the stock fell 2.01% more to 162.85.
signals.what_happened: NVDA closed 162.85 on Nov 13, down 2.01% on 365.8 million shares and 12.75% for the week (Massive). HSBC cut it to Hold and its target to $170 from $365, saying the stock will struggle until a permanent CEO is named, and warned tighter export rules could cut fiscal 2028 earnings per share 13% in its bear case (CNBC; Yahoo Finance). Yahoo Finance counted it as one of at least nine Hold type downgrades since the CEO left. TradingView's 14 day RSI is 24.9, deep in oversold territory, and the stock sits under both its 50 day (214.65) and 200 day (204.19) averages (TradingView). The report is confirmed for Nov 17 after the close (4pm ET); consensus is $2.47 a share on $108.85 billion of revenue (TradingView). Analyst opinion, not our verdict: TradingView lists 57 of 73 analysts at buy or overweight with an average target of $286.12.
signals.so_what: The stock fell because people now pay less for the same earnings, not because estimates fell. That makes Tuesday about two things: whether interim CEO Colette Kress repeats the growth path she gave in August, and whether the board names a permanent CEO. Second order: AMD and AVGO took money from Nvidia this week; a strong Nvidia report could pull that money back. Third order: Nvidia's guide is the best read on AI spending at every supplier on the map (memory, optics, power, cooling). What would make this wrong: a cut guide, or new export limits on Chinese buyers abroad.
signals.for_you: Swing: no NVDA trade before or on the report. Puts: no puts on NVDA, AMD or AVGO before Nov 17; a 10% to 15% move either way is plausible. Long term: NVDA stays 'Wait'. AMD is in its zone but fell 8.75% Friday; wait until after the report for any first tranche.

signals.title: Samsung is reported in talks to buy Modine, a data center cooling chokepoint
signals.what_happened: Bloomberg reported Nov 12 that Samsung Electronics is in talks to acquire Modine Manufacturing, which makes data center chillers and liquid cooling. Neither company confirmed, and no price was reported; Modine was worth about $5.6 billion before the news (Bloomberg; Motley Fool). MOD rose 27.86% to 135.66 on Nov 13 on 8.43 million shares, about 4.5 times normal (Massive; dashboard). Other cooling names fell that day: Vertiv -3.61%, Trane -1.43%, Johnson Controls -2.26% (Massive).
signals.so_what: This is the money trail in action: a chip giant wants to own the cooling that its customers' data centers cannot run without. If a deal happens, it puts a price tag on the cooling layer and could lift other suppliers over time. But the other cooling names fell the same day, so the market is treating this as a one company event. Second order: Samsung buying a US cooling maker may face a national security review, which slows any deal. What would make this wrong: the talks end, or the price is close to Friday's close.
signals.for_you: No action. MOD is on the AI compute map but is not a setup and is in a downtrend on the dashboard; a 28% jump on an unconfirmed deal report is a bet on the deal. VRT has no buy verdict.

signals.title: Trump meets Xi and Putin in Shenzhen on Nov 19; China's metals deadline is Nov 27
signals.what_happened: The White House said Nov 13 that Trump will meet Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin together on Nov 19 at the APEC summit in Shenzhen, which runs Nov 18 to 19 (Bloomberg; BBC). Shenzhen is 13 hours ahead of Eastern time, so the meeting falls on the night of Nov 18 to the early hours of Nov 19 ET; no exact time was given. Separately, China's pause on its ban on gallium, germanium and antimony exports to the US still ends Nov 27, and no extension had been published (InvestorNews; mlq.ai). The broader rare earth pause already runs to Jan 10.
signals.so_what: Markets will read the meeting for three things: chip export rules (Nvidia and the Chinese firms renting chips abroad), the metals deadline, and tariffs. A friendly meeting could extend the metals pause; a cold one could bring back the ban eight days later. Who gets paid if the ban returns: US and allied producers of these metals and their recyclers. Who pays: defense electronics and chip makers that use gallium and germanium. What would make this wrong: the meeting is ceremonial and trade is left to the Jan 10 deadline.
signals.for_you: No action. No Chinese ADR is on the buy list. MP (38.76, Avoid) had an insider cluster on Nov 10 and is the name to watch into Nov 27. Avoid new puts in China exposed names until the meeting is done.

signals.title: Starship Flight 15 reached orbit but skipped the booster catch
signals.what_happened: Starship lifted off from Starbase at 5:48pm CST (6:48pm ET) on Nov 13 and reached orbit on a planned 22 hour flight. SpaceX waved off the booster tower catch and sent Super Heavy to a splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico; it may still try to catch the ship on Nov 14 (Space.com; Spaceflight Now). SPCX closed 139.11 on Nov 13 before the launch, up 3.60% for the week (Massive).
signals.so_what: Reaching orbit again is progress, but cheap launch depends on catching and reflying both stages, and the booster catch was the part that was skipped. Monday's move in SPCX will show how much a ship catch, if it happens, was already priced in.
signals.for_you: No action. SPCX and RKLB are not setups. Watch Monday's open on volume, not the headline.

Puts: expiration week; let out of the money puts expire and roll in the money ones only for a net credit and only if the name is still 'Buy zone now'. No new puts before Nvidia. cycle.quadrant_why: Producer prices rose 6.5% from a year earlier in October (New York Post, Nov 13). Jobless claims are expected at 196,000 next week, near the 200,000 of the prior week (TradingView). Retail sales are forecast to rise again (+0.2%). Growth is firm and prices are hot.
cycle.short_term_debt_cycle: Tightening and late. The Fed's range is 3.75% to 4.00%, about 89% odds of a hike on Dec 9 are priced (CME via InvestmentNews), and the 2 year rose about 42 basis points in a week to 4.88% (FactIQ).
cycle.long_term_debt_cycle: Late. The 10 year closed at 5.15% and the 30 year at 5.47% (Forbes) after two soft long bond sales; a 20 year sale on Nov 18 is the next test. The government pays over 5% to borrow for 10 years or more.
cycle.big_cycle: Debt and money: long yields above 5% and weak auctions. Technology: the largest AI chip maker lost its founder CEO and faces a report with an interim CEO. External order: a Trump, Xi and Putin meeting on Nov 19 and China's metals deadline Nov 27; tanker attacks in the Gulf keep oil near $96.
tailwinds: Breadth improved: the equal weight S&P 500 fund rose 2.37% for the week (Massive).
Producer prices came in a tenth under forecast.
Brent fell for a second week to $95.84.
headwinds: The 10 year at 5.15%, the highest close since Oct 19.
A December hike is about 89% priced.
QQQ closed under its 683.69 line and its 200 day.

history.what: The 10 year briefly passed 5% for the first time since 2007, then fell back the same day (Investopedia, Oct 23, 2023).
history.lesson: A first touch of 5% can mark a peak in yields when growth then cools. The test is whether the next data cools; this time Tuesday's retail sales is the first check.

source.title: Investopedia: 10-year Treasury yield breaches 5% before retreating (Oct 23, 2023)

history.when: February 1994 to February 1995: the Fed's surprise tightening
history.what: The Fed doubled its target from 3% to 6% in a year and US bond losses reached about $600 billion by late 1994 (Fortune).
history.lesson: Weak auctions and rising long yields came before the stock pain. This month has had two weak long sales.

cycle.differences: In 2023 inflation was falling and the Fed was near the end of its hikes. This time producer prices are rising 6.5% a year and the Fed is about to start hiking, so a 5% 10 year is less likely to be the top.
